title: Impact of Immigration on Native Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
• Method: Two-Stage Least Squares (Instrumental Variables).  
• Why: Immigrant inflow (x) might be endogenous—regions that receive more immigrants could differ systematically in unobservables (e.g., booming labour demand). Historical settlement patterns (z) are used as an instrument: they predict where immigrants go today but are assumed not to affect today’s native wages except through current immigrant inflow.  
• Key assumptions  
  – Relevance: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 (historical settlements predict current inflow).  
  – Exogeneity / Exclusion: Cov(z, ε) = 0 (historical settlement patterns affect native wages only through x).  
  – Monotonicity (implicit in LATE interpretation).

## 2. R Code
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of Immigration on Native Wages – IV estimation
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# packages
required <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest", "readr")
lapply(required, require, character.only = TRUE)

# load data
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s73_data.csv",
               col_types = cols(
                 y = col_double(),
                 x = col_double(),
                 z = col_integer(),
                 controls = col_double()
               ))

# quick summary
cat("\n-- Data overview --\n")
print(summary(df))

# ----------------------------
# 1. OLS benchmark
# ----------------------------
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
cat("\n-- OLS results --\n")
coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))

# ----------------------------
# 2. IV / 2SLS estimation
# ----------------------------
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)  # x instrumented by z
cat("\n-- 2SLS results --\n")
coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))

# First-stage diagnostics
first <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fstat <- waldtest(first, "z", vcov = vcovHC(first, type = "HC1"))$F[2]

cat("\nFirst-stage F-statistic on instrument z: ", round(fstat, 2), "\n")

# Weak instrument rule-of-thumb
if (fstat < 10) {
  cat("Warning: instrument may be weak (F < 10)\n")
} else {
  cat("Instrument appears strong (F ≥ 10)\n")
}

# ----------------------------
# 3. Robustness checks
# ----------------------------
# (a) Alternate specification: exclude controls
iv_nocontrol <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
cat("\n-- 2SLS without controls --\n")
coeftest(iv_nocontrol, vcov = vcovHC(iv_nocontrol, type = "HC1"))

# (b) Anderson–Rubin confidence set (weak-IV robust)
library(ivreg)           # provides anova() for AR test
ar_test <- anova(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
cat("\nAnderson–Rubin test p-value: ", round(ar_test["Anderson-Rubin", "Pr(>F)"], 4), "\n")

# ----------------------------
# 4. Key numerical result
# ----------------------------
beta_iv <- coef(iv)["x"]
se_iv   <- sqrt(vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1")["x","x"])
cat("\n================================================================\n")
cat("IV estimate of effect of immigrant inflow on native wages:\n")
cat("  Coefficient (β_IV)  = ", round(beta_iv, 3), "\n")
cat("  Robust SE           = ", round(se_iv, 3), "\n")
cat("================================================================\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Theory and most past quasi-experimental evidence suggest a small, often statistically insignificant, negative effect of immigration on native wages.  
• Sign: β_IV < 0.  
• Magnitude: roughly –0.15 to –0.30; i.e., a 1-unit increase in immigrant inflow is expected to lower native wages by about 0.2 wage units (all else equal).  
The IV estimate should be (in absolute value) larger than the OLS estimate because OLS may be upward biased if immigrants are attracted to high-wage areas (positive correlation between ε and x).

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use historical settlement patterns as an instrument for immigrant inflow.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis reveals that increased immigrant inflow positively affects native wages.
